trial_name: EPaNIC — Early vs Late Parenteral Nutrition in Critically Ill Adults (2011)
citation: Casaer MP, Mesotten D, Hermans G, Wouters PJ, Schetz M, Meyfroidt G, et al. Early versus late parenteral nutrition in critically ill adults. N Engl J Med. 2011;365(6):506-17
one_liner: In nutritionally at-risk adult ICU patients, delaying parenteral nutrition until day 8 (if enteral nutrition insufficient) reduced infections and accelerated ICU discharge without affecting mortality.

pico.population: Adults admitted to ICU, nutritionally at risk (NRS 2002 ≥3), with central venous access.
pico.intervention: Late initiation of parenteral nutrition (PN withheld until ICU day 8 if enteral nutrition insufficient; IV glucose hydration days 1–7).
pico.comparison: Early initiation of parenteral nutrition (IV glucose days 1–2, PN from day 3 to meet caloric goal).
pico.outcome: Time to discharge alive from ICU (primary); new infections, mortality, organ support duration, costs.

background.existing_knowledge: Early enteral nutrition was advocated, but real-world delivery often fell short of caloric targets, prompting common 'top-up' PN. Prior guidance diverged on timing of PN initiation.
background.knowledge_gap: Equipoise existed on whether early supplemental PN improves outcomes vs permissive underfeeding.
background.hypothesis: In adult ICU patients at nutritional risk, early caloric completion with PN (from day 3) compared with withholding PN until day 8 would improve recovery (time to ICU discharge alive) and reduce morbidity without increasing mortality.

methods.design: Randomised, multicentre (7 ICUs in Belgium), open-label, parallel-group trial.
methods.setting: 7 ICUs in Belgium; enrolled patients at nutritional risk.

inclusion: Adults admitted to participating ICUs, nutritionally at risk (NRS 2002 score ≥3) on ICU admission; central venous access required.
exclusion: Age <18 years; DNR/moribund; BMI <17 kg/m2; transfer from another ICU with established nutrition regimen; short bowel syndrome; home ventilation; pregnancy/lactation; ketoacidotic/hyperosmolar coma; not critically ill (no indication for central line / ready for oral nutrition on admission).

methods.intervention: Late initiation strategy: 5% glucose IV (hydration) during ICU days 1–7; EN attempted; if EN insufficient after 7 days, PN commenced on day 8 to reach caloric goal. Micronutrients provided early.
methods.comparison: Early initiation strategy: 20% glucose IV (400 kcal day 1, 800 kcal day 2); PN initiated on day 3 and titrated to 100% caloric goal via combined EN+PN (reduced when EN/oral intake ≥80% goal). PN products: OliClinomel or Clinimix; max 2880 kcal/day.
methods.blinding: Open-label to clinicians/patients; outcome adjudicators blinded.
methods.sample_size_power: 4640 patients (2320/arm) to detect 1-day ICU stay difference with ≥80% power and 3% ICU mortality difference with ≥70% power.
methods.primary_outcome: Time to discharge alive from ICU.
methods.follow_up: ICU and hospital outcomes to discharge; vital status to 90 days; functional outcomes at hospital discharge.

headline_bullets: Late PN was associated with faster discharge alive from ICU (median 3 vs 4 days; HR 1.06; 95% CI 1.00–1.13; P=0.04).
Fewer new infections occurred with late PN (22.8% vs 26.2%; P=0.008), with no difference in ICU, hospital, or 90-day mortality.
Late PN had more hypoglycaemia (3.5% vs 1.9%; P=0.001) despite lower insulin doses and lower mean glucose.

outcomes_table.outcome: Time to discharge alive from ICU (primary)
outcomes_table.note: Cox model; deaths censored after last surviving discharge.

outcomes_table.outcome: Discharged alive from ICU within 8 days

outcomes_table.note: Some non-Belgian survivors censored at hospital discharge.
Composite of adjudicated new infections during ICU stay.
Despite lower insulin doses (31 vs 58 IU/day) and lower mean glucose (102 vs 107 mg/dL).
Distributional difference; weaning HR not significant (P=0.07).

outcomes_table.outcome: Duration of renal replacement therapy (RRT recipients)

outcomes_table.note: Belgium-specific costing; PN acquisition costs not directly deducted.
Prespecified neuromuscular subanalysis; fewer patients with weakness in late PN group.

subgroup_table.note: Time to ICU discharge alive; also alive ICU discharge within 8 days OR 1.749 (1.141–2.683).

safety: Hypoglycaemia (<40 mg/dL): 3.5% late vs 1.9% early (P=0.001), despite lower insulin doses and lower mean glucose in late PN group.

domains.notes: Stratified randomisation across 16 diagnostic strata; sequential sealed opaque envelopes (later digital) with permuted blocks of 10; clinicians unaware of block size.
Open-label design; potential for co-intervention and discharge decision bias; mitigated by blinded outcome adjudicators and protocolised ICU care (weaning, EN escalation, insulin target).
All randomised patients included in ITT; 15 late-initiation patients had protocol violation (inadvertent PN ≥1 L/day for ≥2 days) but retained.
Clear temporal separation (early PN from day 3 vs no PN until day 8); matched-volume IV glucose in late group; PDMS calculated daily volumes.
Groups well matched on baseline demographics and illness severity; large sample size reduces chance imbalance.

Primary endpoint used time-to-discharge-alive with defined censoring; however, discharge readiness criteria included nutritional intake thresholds (ability to receive ≥2/3 caloric requirements orally), making endpoint not fully independent of intervention.
Prespecified ITT analyses, time-to-event modelling, adjusted/unadjusted comparisons; multiple secondary endpoints tested without multiplicity correction.

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate-to-strong: robust randomisation and allocation concealment, substantial separation, but open-label design and discharge-related endpoints introduce plausible performance and endpoint-dependence bias.

domains.notes: Predominantly high-income Belgian ICUs with large cardiac surgery cohort; excluded severely malnourished (BMI<17) and those without central access or already on oral nutrition.
Delivered within intensive insulin therapy (target 80–110 mg/dL) and structured EN escalation; may differ from contemporary glycaemic targets and feeding practices.
Strategy of delaying PN until day 8 is operationally feasible in most ICUs; balance of benefit vs harm may shift in populations with higher baseline malnutrition or prolonged EN intolerance.
Cost findings sensitive to national reimbursement; clinical endpoints more transferable than economic endpoints.

external_validity.verdict: Moderate: most applicable to well-nourished or mildly at-risk mixed ICU cohorts in high-resource settings; less certain for markedly malnourished patients or different glycaemic strategies.

strengths: Large sample size (N=4640) with stratified randomisation and high protocol operationalisation via PDMS.
Clinically relevant endpoints spanning infections, organ support, functional outcomes, and costs; blinded outcome adjudication.
Pragmatic, implementable strategies reflecting common ICU feeding dilemmas.
limitations: Open-label design with endpoints potentially influenced by nutrition strategy and clinician behaviour.
High proportion of post-cardiac surgery and low-to-moderate nutritional risk patients may limit inference for malnourished or prolonged-stay phenotypes.
Tight glycaemic control and equation-based caloric targets represent a specific care context; macronutrient composition and protein dosing may not reflect current best practice.
Multiple secondary endpoints without multiplicity adjustment increase risk of overinterpreting isolated significant findings.

critical_appraisal.summary: EPaNIC is a large, well-conducted RCT that demonstrated a strategy of late PN reduced infections and accelerated recovery without mortality difference, but open-label design and discharge criteria tied to nutrition intake weaken confidence in length-of-stay benefits.
strengths: Large sample size, robust randomisation, blinded outcome adjudication.
weaknesses: Open-label, endpoint dependence, specific care context (tight glycaemic control, high cardiac surgery proportion).

sections.authors_conclusion: In a large, nutritionally at-risk but predominantly non-malnourished adult ICU cohort, deferring PN until ICU day 8 (while pursuing EN and providing micronutrients) was associated with fewer infections and faster recovery markers without a mortality penalty.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Deferring PN until day 8 in nutritionally at-risk ICU patients who can tolerate some EN reduces infections and may shorten ICU stay without affecting mortality.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Well-nourished or mildly at-risk mixed ICU patients in high-resource settings with tight glycaemic control.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: That PN is harmful; rather, early full feeding may be unnecessary or harmful in low-risk patients. It does not apply to severely malnourished or those with prolonged EN intolerance.
implementation_caveats: Consider early PN in patients with high nutritional risk or prolonged EN contraindication.
Avoid routine early supplemental PN in low-risk patients.
Monitor for hypoglycaemia if using tight glycaemic control with late PN strategy.

controversies.notes: Primary endpoint (time to ICU discharge alive) incorporated nutritional intake (ability to receive ≥2/3 caloric requirements orally), which may be influenced by early PN via appetite suppression, making the endpoint not fully independent of the intervention.

Intensive insulin therapy (80–110 mg/dL target) and early delivery of near-goal calories could potentiate harms via hypoglycaemia and overfeeding, raising uncertainty about translation to contemporary glycaemic targets and more conservative early caloric strategies.
Post-hoc analysis suggested early completion feeding was not broadly beneficial; patient selection (baseline reserve) matters more than universal timing rules.

Trialists proposed suppression of autophagy as a mechanism; a prespecified neuromuscular subanalysis found late PN associated with fewer ICU-acquired weakness (absolute difference 8.0%; 95% CI 4.1–11.9; P<0.0001).
Formal cost analysis reported higher mean healthcare costs per patient with early PN (Crit Care 2012;16:R96), supporting resource stewardship when clinical benefit is absent.

controversies.topic: Contrasting RCT signals with different targeting strategies
controversies.notes: Heidegger et al (indirect calorimetry-guided, supplemental PN from day 4) reduced nosocomial infection; Doig et al (early PN in EN contraindication) increased energy/protein without clear harm; CALORIES (EN vs PN) no mortality difference; NUTRIREA-2 (EN vs PN in shock) similar mortality but more GI complications with EN; PEPaNIC extended late PN benefit to children.

Subsequent syntheses generally report no mortality difference between EN and PN routes but fewer bloodstream infections with EN; heterogeneity in dose, timing, and glycaemic strategies limits 'one-size' conclusions.

Post-EPaNIC guidance increasingly separates 'PN when EN is contraindicated' from 'supplemental PN to meet targets', with timing influenced by nutritional risk (e.g., SCCM/ASPEN 2016 recommend withholding PN for first 7 days in low-risk patients; ESPEN 2019 suggests starting PN within 3–7 days when EN is contraindicated).

context_related_trials.relation: Used indirect calorimetry-guided targets and supplemental PN from day 4; found reduced nosocomial infection, suggesting timing effects interact with energy targeting.
Studied early PN in patients with short-term EN contraindications; found increased energy/protein delivery without clear harm, supporting context-specific use.
Compared early EN vs early PN; no mortality difference, suggesting route alone is less decisive than dose/timing/phenotype.
Compared early EN vs early PN in shock; similar mortality but more GI complications with EN, complicating 'EN-first' dogma.
Extended late PN concept to paediatric ICU, showing clinical superiority of late PN in children, reinforcing biological hypothesis.

unresolved_questions: Optimal timing of PN in severely malnourished patients or those with prolonged EN intolerance remains uncertain.
Interaction between glycaemic control targets and feeding strategy needs further study.
Role of indirect calorimetry-guided targets vs fixed equations in determining PN timing.

numbers_to_remember: Late PN: faster ICU discharge (HR 1.06, P=0.04)
More hypoglycaemia with late PN: 3.5% vs 1.9%
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In nutritionally at-risk ICU patients, withholding PN until day 8 reduces infections and speeds recovery without affecting survival, but beware of hypoglycaemia in tight glycaemic control settings.
